The LBM is validated for electromagnetic scattering across one-, two-, and three-dimensional configurations.
The study covers size parameters from 0.125 (Rayleigh regime) to 314 (geometric optics regime).
LBM results for PEC circular cylinders show excellent agreement with analytical Mie theory across all size parameters.
Dielectric cylinders with relative permittivities ranging from 1 to 200 are tested, showing deviations close to 1% in reflection and transmission at planar interfaces.
The D3Q7 lattice is used for discretizing Maxwell’s equations in the LBM framework.
The LBM scheme is second-order accurate in space and time.
Near-to-far-field transformation uses equivalent electric and magnetic surface currents derived from recorded near-field data on a fictitious boundary.
LBM can accurately model scattering from hexagonal dielectric cylinders, validated against the Discretized Mie-Formalism.
The speed of light in lattice units is c = 1/3, leading to a factor of 3 in the recovered Maxwell’s curl equations.
LBM requires about three times more memory and six times longer computation time than FDTD for equal spatial resolution but fewer lattice points for the same accuracy.
The computational domain size and grid resolution are adapted based on the size-to-wavelength ratio for efficient simulations.
The LBM solver is implemented in C with OpenMP parallelization and controlled via Python for flexibility.
Scattering width (SW) in 2D has units of length, while radar cross section (RCS) in 3D has units of area.
Open boundary conditions are applied in LBM to suppress spurious reflections at domain boundaries.
The method handles both perfect electrically conducting (PEC) and dielectric materials with arbitrary relative permittivities.
The study is the first systematic benchmarking of LBM for electromagnetic scattering across canonical and non-canonical shapes.
LBM can capture complex boundary effects such as edge diffraction and sharp facets.
The NTFF transformation involves Fourier transforming time-domain fields to frequency domain before computing far-field quantities.
The incident wave is typically a transverse magnetic (TMz) polarized plane wave in 2D cylinder scattering simulations.
The study includes validation against exact Mie solutions for dielectric spheres in 3D.
